chapters.title: Chapter I
paragraphs: 1801—I have just come back from visiting my landlord—the only neighbour I shall have to put up with. This is certainly beautiful country! Nowhere in England, I believe, could I have chosen a place so entirely cut off from the bustle of society. A perfect heaven for a man who hates company—and Mr. Heathcliff and I make an excellent pair to share its desolation. A splendid fellow! He had no idea how warmly I felt towards him when, as I rode up, I saw his black eyes retreat so suspiciously beneath their brows, and when, on hearing my name, his fingers burrowed still deeper into his waistcoat, determined to guard their privacy.
“Mr. Heathcliff?” I asked.
He answered with a nod.

“Mr. Lockwood, sir, your new tenant. I have the honour of paying my respects as soon as I can after arriving, and hope I have not inconvenienced you by asking so persistently to rent Thrushcross Grange: I heard yesterday that you had been considering—”
“Thrushcross Grange belongs to me, sir,” he cut in, with a wince. “I would let nobody inconvenience me if I could prevent it—come in!”

His “come in” emerged through clenched teeth and meant, plainly enough, “Go to the Devil!” Even the gate he leaned on showed no inclination to support the invitation by moving; and I think that decided me to accept it. I was interested in a man who seemed to carry reserve even further than I did myself.

Once he saw my horse's chest actually pressing against the gate, he reached out to unfasten its chain, then led me sullenly up the paved path. As we entered the courtyard he called, “Joseph, take Mr. Lockwood's horse; and bring us some wine.”

“That must be the entire household staff, I suppose,” I reflected on hearing these combined instructions. “No wonder grass grows between the paving stones, and the hedges have only cattle to trim them.”

Joseph was elderly—no, old; very old, perhaps, though vigorous and wiry. “The Lord help us!” he muttered to himself in a low, peevishly disapproving voice as he took my horse. Meanwhile, he gave my face so sour a look that I generously supposed he needed divine assistance to digest his dinner, and that his pious outburst had nothing to do with my unexpected arrival.

Mr. Heathcliff's house is called Wuthering Heights. “Wuthering” is an expressive local word for the atmospheric uproar to which its exposed position subjects it in stormy weather. They must indeed have plenty of fresh, bracing air up there at all times: you can judge the strength of the north wind sweeping over the ridge by the extreme tilt of a few stunted fir trees beside the house, and by a row of gaunt thorns stretching their branches all one way, as though begging the sun for charity. Fortunately, the architect had the foresight to make it solid: the narrow windows are set deep in the walls, and great projecting stones protect the corners.

Before stepping inside, I stopped to admire the fantastic carvings scattered lavishly across the front, particularly round the main doorway. Above it, among a wilderness of crumbling griffins and shameless little boys, I made out the date “1500” and the name “Hareton Earnshaw.” I would have offered a few observations and asked the ill-tempered owner for a brief history of the place; but his stance in the doorway seemed to demand that I either come in immediately or leave altogether. I did not want to try his patience further before inspecting the inner sanctuary.

A single step took us into the family sitting room, without any preliminary hall or passage. Here they call this principal room “the house.” It generally serves as both kitchen and parlour; but at Wuthering Heights I think the kitchen has been driven into a separate part of the building altogether. At any rate, I could hear voices chattering and cooking utensils rattling far inside, and saw no signs of roasting, boiling or baking around the enormous fireplace, nor copper pans and tin colanders shining on the walls. At one end, however, both light and heat were splendidly reflected by ranks of huge pewter dishes, with silver jugs and tankards between them, rising in row upon row on a vast oak dresser right up to the roof. There was no ceiling beneath that roof: its whole structure lay exposed to an inquisitive eye, except where a wooden rack loaded with oatcakes and bunches of legs of beef, mutton and ham hid it. Above the fireplace hung several evil-looking old guns and a pair of horse pistols; three brightly painted tins arranged on the mantelpiece supplied the decoration. The floor was smooth white stone. The chairs were primitive, high-backed things painted green, with one or two heavy black ones lurking in the shadows. A huge liver-coloured female pointer lay in an arched recess beneath the dresser, surrounded by a swarm of squealing puppies; other dogs occupied the remaining corners.

The room and its furniture would have been perfectly ordinary possessions for a plain northern farmer, a stubborn-faced man whose sturdy legs showed well in knee breeches and gaiters. You may see such a man sitting in his armchair, a mug of frothing ale on the round table before him, anywhere within five or six miles of these hills, if you arrive at the right time after dinner. But Mr. Heathcliff presents a striking contrast to his home and way of life. In appearance he is a dark-skinned gypsy; in clothes and manners, a gentleman—that is, as much of one as many a country squire. He may be somewhat untidy, but his neglect does not look bad on him, for he stands straight and has a handsome figure; and he is rather sullen. Some people might suspect a touch of ill-bred pride. Something sympathetic within me says it is nothing of the kind: I know instinctively that his reserve comes from a dislike of showy feelings—of demonstrations of mutual goodwill. He will conceal his love and hatred equally, and think it something of an impertinence to be loved or hated in return. No, I am getting ahead of myself: I am much too ready to give him my own characteristics. Mr. Heathcliff may have entirely different reasons from mine for keeping his hand out of reach when someone hopes to make his acquaintance. Let me hope that my disposition is almost unique: my dear mother used to say I would never have a comfortable home; and only last summer I proved myself completely unworthy of one.

During a month of fine weather at the seaside, I found myself in the company of a most fascinating creature: a true goddess in my eyes, so long as she took no notice of me. I “never told my love” aloud; yet, if looks can speak, the greatest idiot could have guessed that I was head over heels. At last she understood, and answered with a look—the sweetest look anyone could imagine. And what did I do? I confess it with shame: I withdrew icily into myself, like a snail. With every glance I retreated further and grew colder, until the poor innocent finally began to distrust her own senses and, overwhelmed with embarrassment at her supposed mistake, persuaded her mother to leave.
This curious twist in my character has earned me a reputation for intentional heartlessness. Only I can understand how little I deserve it.

I sat down at the opposite end of the hearth from the one my landlord approached, and tried to fill a silence by stroking the mother dog. She had left her puppies and was creeping wolfishly behind my legs, lip curled, white teeth watering for a bite. My friendly touch brought out a long growl deep in her throat.

“You'd best leave the dog alone,” Mr. Heathcliff growled in accompaniment, stopping her more threatening movements with a thrust of his foot. “She isn't used to being fussed over—we don't keep her as a pet.” Then he strode to a side door and shouted once more, “Joseph!”

From the depths of the cellar Joseph muttered something indistinct, but showed no sign of coming up. His master therefore plunged down after him, leaving me _vis-à-vis_ the ruffianly bitch and two grim, shaggy sheepdogs, who joined her in jealously watching every movement I made. Having no wish to meet their fangs, I kept still; but I imagined they could hardly understand insults delivered in silence, and unfortunately began winking and pulling faces at the three of them. Some twist of my features so offended madam that she flew into a sudden rage and jumped onto my knees. I threw her off and hurried to get the table between us. This action stirred up the whole hive: half a dozen four-legged devils, of different ages and sizes, came out of hidden dens and converged on the same spot. My heels and coat tails seemed particularly singled out for attack; and while I kept the bigger fighters off with the poker as well as I could, I was forced to call loudly for someone in the household to help restore peace.

Mr. Heathcliff and his servant climbed the cellar steps with infuriating calm. I doubt they moved a second faster than usual, although the hearth was a perfect storm of snapping and yelping. Fortunately someone in the kitchen acted more quickly: a vigorous woman with her dress tucked up, her arms bare and her cheeks red from the fire rushed among us brandishing a frying pan. She used this weapon and her tongue so effectively that the storm subsided as if by magic. When her master appeared, she alone remained in motion, heaving like the sea after a gale.
“What the devil is going on?” he demanded, looking me over in a way I could hardly bear after such an inhospitable reception.
“What the devil indeed!” I muttered. “The herd of possessed swine can't have held worse spirits than these animals of yours, sir. You might as well abandon a stranger among a litter of tigers!”
“They leave people alone if people leave things alone,” he observed, setting the bottle in front of me and putting the table back. “Quite right of the dogs to keep watch. A glass of wine?”
“No, thank you.”
“You haven't been bitten?”
“If I had, I'd have left my own mark on the biter.” Heathcliff's face loosened into a grin.

“Come now,” he said, “you're upset, Mr. Lockwood. Here, have a little wine. Visitors are so extraordinarily uncommon in this house that my dogs and I, I'll readily admit, scarcely know how to welcome them. Your health, sir?”

I bowed and drank to his health in return, beginning to see how foolish it would be to sit sulking over the bad behaviour of a pack of mongrels. Besides, since his humour ran that way, I was unwilling to give the fellow any further amusement at my expense. He—probably reflecting sensibly that offending a good tenant would be foolish—relaxed somewhat his clipped manner of speech, with its missing pronouns and helping verbs, and began what he supposed would interest me: a discussion of the merits and drawbacks of my present retreat. He knew a great deal about the subjects we touched on; and by the time I left for home I felt encouraged enough to offer to visit again tomorrow. He clearly had no wish for me to intrude a second time. Nevertheless, I shall go. It is astonishing how sociable I feel when I compare myself with him.

chapters.title: Chapter II
paragraphs: Yesterday afternoon turned cold and misty. I was half inclined to spend it by the fire in my study, rather than struggle through heather and mud to Wuthering Heights. But when I came upstairs after dinner—note that I dine between twelve and one: the housekeeper, a motherly woman who came with the house as part of its equipment, either could not or would not understand my request to be served at five—when, I say, I went upstairs with this idle plan and entered the room, I found a servant girl kneeling among brushes and coal scuttles, raising a hellish cloud of dust as she smothered the flames with heaps of cinders. The sight drove me straight out again. I took my hat, walked four miles, and reached Heathcliff's garden gate just in time to avoid the first feathery flakes of a snow shower.

Up on that bleak hilltop a dry frost had hardened the ground, and the air sent shivers through every limb. I could not undo the chain, so I climbed over and ran up the paved path between straggling gooseberry bushes. I knocked in vain for someone to let me in, until my knuckles tingled and the dogs began to howl.

“Miserable inhabitants!” I exclaimed inwardly. “For such boorish inhospitality you deserve to be cut off from the human race for ever. At least I would not bar my doors in broad daylight. I don't care—I will get inside!” With this determination I grabbed the latch and shook it violently. Joseph's vinegar face emerged from a round window in the barn.
“What d'ye want?” he shouted. “T' master's down in t' yard. Go round t' end o' t' barn if ye want to speak to him.”
“Isn't there anyone in the house who can open up?” I shouted back.
“There's nobbut t' missis; and she won't open it, though ye make that frightful din till night.”
“Why not? Can't you tell her who I am, Joseph?”
“Not me! I'll have no hand in it,” the head muttered, and disappeared.

The snow began blowing thickly. I caught hold of the handle for another attempt, just as a young man in his shirtsleeves, carrying a pitchfork on his shoulder, appeared in the yard behind me. He called to me to follow him. After going through a washhouse and a paved yard containing a coal shed, a pump and a pigeon house, we finally reached the great warm, welcoming room where I had been received before. It shone delightfully in the light of an enormous fire of coal, peat and wood; and beside a table laid for a generous evening meal I was pleased to see the “missis,” whose existence I had never even suspected. I bowed and waited, expecting her to invite me to sit. Leaning back in her chair, she looked at me without moving or speaking.
“Terrible weather!” I observed. “I'm afraid, Mrs. Heathcliff, your door will have suffered from the leisurely way your servants answer it: I had quite a struggle to make them hear.”
She did not open her mouth. I stared, and she stared too—or at least kept her eyes fixed on me with a cold indifference that was exceedingly unpleasant and embarrassing.
“Take a seat,” the young man said roughly. “He'll be here shortly.”
I did as he said, cleared my throat and called the villain Juno, who on this second meeting graciously moved the very tip of her tail to acknowledge our acquaintance.
“What a fine animal!” I tried again. “Will you be finding homes for the puppies, madam?”
“They don't belong to me,” said my charming hostess, with more hostility than even Heathcliff could have managed.
“Ah, perhaps these are your favourites?” I continued, turning towards a shadowy cushion covered with what looked like cats.
“An odd choice of favourites that would be!” she said contemptuously.
Unfortunately they were a pile of dead rabbits. I cleared my throat again, moved nearer the fire, and repeated my observation about the wild evening.
“You ought to have stayed at home,” she said, getting up and reaching for two of the painted tins on the mantelpiece.

Before, her seat had kept her out of the light; now I could see her entire face and figure clearly. She was slender, and seemed barely past girlhood: a lovely figure, and the most exquisite little face I have ever had the pleasure of seeing. Her features were small and very fair; flaxen curls—or golden, rather—hung loose over her delicate neck. Her eyes, if their expression had been pleasant, would have been irresistible. Fortunately for my easily touched heart, the only feeling they showed lay somewhere between scorn and a sort of despair, strangely out of place in such eyes. The tins were almost beyond her reach; I moved to help, and she turned on me as a miser might turn on someone who offered to help him count his gold.
“I need no help from you,” she snapped. “I can reach them myself.”
“Please forgive me!” I replied hastily.
“Has anyone invited you to tea?” she demanded, fastening an apron over her neat black dress and holding a spoonful of tea leaves above the pot.
“I'd be very glad of a cup,” I replied.
“Have you been invited?” she asked again.
“No,” I answered with half a smile. “That invitation would properly come from you.”
She threw the tea back, spoon and all, and returned to her chair in a sulk, her forehead creased and her red lower lip thrust out like a child's on the verge of tears.

Meanwhile the young man had thrown on an unmistakably shabby coat and stationed himself upright before the fire. He looked down at me out of the corners of his eyes exactly as if some deadly feud between us remained unavenged. I began to wonder whether he was a servant. Both his clothes and his speech were rough, entirely lacking the refinement visible in Mr. and Mrs. Heathcliff. His thick brown curls were untidy and unkempt, his whiskers spread bearishly across his cheeks, and his hands were browned like an ordinary labourer's. Yet his manner was unconstrained, almost proud, and he showed none of a servant's diligence in attending to the lady of the house. With no clear evidence of his position, I thought it best to ignore his strange behaviour. Five minutes later Heathcliff came in, relieving my discomfort to some extent.
“You see, sir, I've kept my promise and come!” I exclaimed, putting on a cheerful manner. “And I'm afraid the weather may keep me here for half an hour, if you can give me shelter for that long.”

“Half an hour?” he said, shaking the white flakes off his clothes. “I'm amazed you chose the middle of a snowstorm for a walk. Do you realise you could lose yourself in the marshes? Even people who know these moors often go astray on evenings like this, and I can tell you there's no prospect of a change just now.”
“Perhaps one of your lads could guide me, and stay at the Grange until morning—could you spare someone?”
“No, I couldn't.”
“Oh, really! Well then, I shall have to rely on my own good sense.”
“Humph!”
“Are ye going to make t' tea?” demanded the wearer of the shabby coat, transferring his ferocious stare from me to the young woman.
“Does _he_ get any?” she asked Heathcliff for a decision.

“Will you get it ready?” he answered, so savagely that I flinched. The way he spoke exposed a truly vicious nature. I no longer felt like calling Heathcliff a splendid fellow. Once everything was prepared, he invited me with, “Now, sir, bring your chair up.” We all drew round the table, the country youth included, and a forbidding silence held while we dealt with our meal.

I thought that if I had brought this cloud over them, I ought to try to clear it. Surely they could not sit in such grim silence every day; however bad-tempered they might be, the scowl on every face could not possibly be their ordinary expression.

“It's curious,” I began, between finishing one cup of tea and receiving the next, “how habit can shape our tastes and ideas. Many people could not imagine happiness in a life as completely cut off from the world as yours, Mr. Heathcliff; yet I venture to say that, surrounded by your family, with your charming wife the guiding spirit of your home and heart—”
“My charming wife!” he interrupted, his face twisted into an almost devilish sneer. “And where is she—my charming wife?”
“I mean Mrs. Heathcliff, your wife.”
“Well, yes—oh, you mean her spirit has become a guardian angel, watching over the fortunes of Wuthering Heights although her body has gone. Is that your meaning?”

Realising I had blundered, I tried to put it right. I might have noticed that the difference in their ages made it unlikely they were husband and wife. One was about forty, an age of mental vigour when men seldom delude themselves that girls marry them for love: that dream is kept to comfort our declining years. The other did not look seventeen.

Then the answer struck me. “That rustic at my elbow, drinking tea from a basin and eating bread with unwashed hands, may be her husband: Heathcliff junior, of course. This is what comes of being buried alive: she has wasted herself on that boor because she simply doesn't know that better men exist! What a pity—I must take care not to make her regret her choice.” That last thought may sound conceited; it was not. The man beside me seemed almost repulsive, while I knew from experience that I was reasonably attractive.

“Mrs. Heathcliff is my daughter-in-law,” Heathcliff said, confirming my guess. As he spoke, he gave her a peculiar look: a look of hatred, unless his facial muscles work in some very perverse way and, unlike other people's, refuse to express what is in his soul.
“Ah, of course—I understand now: you are the fortunate owner of this kindly fairy,” I remarked, turning to the man beside me.

This was worse than my earlier mistake. The youth turned crimson and clenched his fist, looking thoroughly ready to attack me. But he apparently recovered himself a moment later and choked back his anger with a savage curse muttered for my benefit—which, however, I carefully pretended not to hear.

“Your guesses are unfortunate, sir,” my host observed. “Neither of us enjoys the privilege of possessing your good fairy; her husband is dead. I said she was my daughter-in-law, so she must have married my son.”
“And this young gentleman is—”
“Certainly no son of mine.”
Heathcliff smiled once more, as though suggesting he had fathered that bear was rather too audacious a joke.
“I'm Hareton Earnshaw,” the other man growled, “and I'd advise you to treat that name with respect!”
“I haven't shown it any disrespect,” I answered, privately amused at the dignity of his announcement.

He kept his eyes on me longer than I wished to meet them, for fear I might be tempted either to box his ears or to laugh aloud. I began to feel decidedly out of place in this agreeable family gathering. The gloomy atmosphere of their spirits overwhelmed and more than cancelled out the warm comforts surrounding me, and I resolved to think carefully before venturing beneath that roof a third time.

When the business of eating was finished, and nobody offered a word of friendly conversation, I went to a window to inspect the weather. The sight was dismal: darkness falling before its time, and sky and hills merging in one bitter whirl of wind and smothering snow.
“I really don't think I can get home now without someone to guide me,” I could not help exclaiming. “The roads must be buried already; and even if they weren't, I could scarcely see a foot ahead.”
“Hareton, get those twelve sheep under the barn porch. They'll be buried if they're left in the pen all night, and put a plank across in front of them,” Heathcliff said.
“What am I supposed to do?” I persisted, growing irritated.

Nobody answered my question. Looking round, I saw only Joseph carrying in a bucket of porridge for the dogs, and Mrs. Heathcliff bent over the fire, amusing herself by burning a bundle of matches that had fallen from the mantelpiece when she put back the tea tin. Having set his load down, Joseph surveyed the room disapprovingly and rasped in his cracked voice, “I wonder how ye can bring yerself to stand there doing nowt and worse, when all t' others have gone out! But ye're a good-for-nowt, and talking's no use—ye'll never mend yer wicked ways, but go straight to t' devil, like yer mother before ye!”
For a moment I thought this eloquent speech was meant for me. Angry enough, I stepped towards the old rogue with the intention of kicking him out of the door; but Mrs. Heathcliff's reply stopped me.

“You disgraceful old hypocrite!” she answered. “Aren't you afraid of being carried off, body and all, every time you speak the devil's name? Take care how you provoke me, or I'll ask him to abduct you as a particular favour! Wait! Look here, Joseph,” she went on, taking a long, dark book off a shelf. “I'll show you how much I've learned of the Black Art: soon I'll know enough to clear the whole house. That red cow didn't die by accident, and your rheumatism can hardly be put down to the workings of Providence!”
“Oh, wicked, wicked!” the old man gasped. “May t' Lord deliver us from evil!”

“No, sinner! You're already damned—get out, or I'll do you real harm! I'll make images of every one of you in wax and clay! And the first to cross the boundaries I set shall—I won't tell you what will happen to him—but you'll see! Go on, I'm watching you!”

The little witch put a pretence of malice into her lovely eyes. Joseph hurried out trembling with very real horror, praying and exclaiming “wicked” as he went. I supposed she was indulging in some sort of bleak amusement; and now we were alone I tried to interest her in my predicament.

“Mrs. Heathcliff,” I said earnestly, “forgive me for troubling you. I take the liberty because I'm certain someone with your face must be kind-hearted. Please point out some landmarks so I can find my way home: I know no more about getting there than you would about finding your way to London!”
“Go back the way you came,” she replied, settling into a chair with a candle and the long book open before her. “It's short advice, but the best I can offer.”
“So if you hear they've found me dead in a bog or a snow-filled pit, your conscience won't suggest you were partly to blame?”
“Why should it? I can't go with you. They wouldn't let me as far as the end of the garden wall.”
“_You_! I'd be sorry to ask you to step outside for my sake on a night like this,” I cried. “I want you to _tell_ me the way, not _show_ me: or persuade Mr. Heathcliff to let me have a guide.”
“Who? There's him, Earnshaw, Zillah, Joseph and me. Which one do you want?”
“Don't you have any boys working on the farm?”
“No. That's everyone.”
“Then it seems I have no choice but to stay.”
“You'll have to arrange that with your host. It's no concern of mine.”

“I hope this teaches you not to go wandering recklessly over these hills again,” came Heathcliff's harsh voice from the kitchen doorway. “As for staying, I don't provide rooms for visitors: you'll have to share a bed with Hareton or Joseph.”
“A chair in this room would do for me to sleep in,” I replied.
“No, no! Rich or poor, a stranger's still a stranger. It doesn't suit me to let anyone roam about the place when I'm not there to watch!” said the ill-mannered brute.

That insult exhausted my patience. I expressed my disgust and pushed past him into the yard, colliding with Earnshaw in my hurry. It was too dark to see the way out, and as I searched round I heard another example of their courteous behaviour to one another. At first the young man seemed inclined to help me.
“I'll take him as far as the park,” he said.
“You can take him to hell!” exclaimed his master, or whatever he was to him. “And who'll see to the horses, eh?”
“A man's life matters more than leaving the horses for one evening: someone must go,” Mrs. Heathcliff murmured, with more kindness than I had expected.
“Not because you order it!” Hareton shot back. “If you care about him, you'd do better to keep quiet.”
“Then I hope his ghost comes back to haunt you, and I hope Mr. Heathcliff gets no more tenants until the Grange falls to pieces,” she answered sharply.
“Listen, listen, she's putting a curse on 'em!” muttered Joseph, towards whom I had been making my way.
He was sitting within hearing, milking the cows by lantern light. Without ceremony I seized the lantern and, calling out that I would return it tomorrow, rushed towards the nearest small gate.
“Master, master, he's stealing t' lantern!” the old man shouted, chasing after me. “Hey, Gnasher! Hey, dog! Hey, Wolf, hold him, hold him!”

As I opened the little door, two hairy monsters sprang at my throat, knocked me down and put out the light. Heathcliff and Hareton's mingled laughter crowned my fury and humiliation. Fortunately, the animals seemed more interested in stretching their paws, yawning and wagging their tails than in eating me alive; but they would allow no rising from the dead, and I had to lie there until their spiteful masters chose to release me. Then, hatless and shaking with anger, I ordered the villains to let me out, and warned them they kept me another minute at their peril. I added several confused threats of revenge which, in their vague depths of venom, had a flavour of King Lear.

The violence of my agitation brought on a heavy nosebleed; still Heathcliff laughed, and still I raged. I don't know how the scene would have ended if someone rather more sensible than I, and more kindly than my host, had not been nearby. This was Zillah, the stout housekeeper, who finally came out to discover what the commotion meant. She thought some of them had been attacking me, and, not daring to turn on her master, aimed her verbal artillery at the younger scoundrel.

“Well, Mr. Earnshaw,” she cried, “whatever will ye be up to next? Are we to murder folk on our own doorstep? I can see this house'll never suit me—look at t' poor lad, he's fair choking! Hush, hush; ye mustn't carry on so. Come inside and I'll put that right: there now, keep yerself still.”

With that she suddenly poured a pint of ice-cold water down my neck and dragged me into the kitchen. Mr. Heathcliff came after us, his chance burst of amusement quickly fading into his customary sullenness.

I felt terribly sick, dizzy and faint, and so had no choice but to accept a night's lodging under his roof. He told Zillah to give me a glass of brandy, then went through to the inner room. She sympathised with my miserable state and, after obeying his orders—which revived me a little—showed me to bed.

chapters.title: Chapter III
paragraphs: As she led me upstairs, she advised me to hide the candle and make no noise. Her master had a strange feeling about the bedroom she was taking me to, and never willingly allowed anyone to sleep there. I asked why. She did not know, she said: she had lived there only a year or two, and so many odd things went on that she could not begin to wonder about them.

Too dazed to feel curious myself, I secured the door and looked round for the bed. The entire furniture was a chair, a wardrobe and a large oak box, with square openings near its top like the windows of a coach. I went over and looked inside. It proved to be a peculiar old-fashioned bed, cleverly designed to save every member of the family from needing a separate room. In effect it made a little enclosed chamber, and the sill of a window contained within it served as a table.
I slid the panelled sides back, climbed in with my candle, and closed them again, feeling safe from Heathcliff's watchfulness and everyone else's.

The window ledge where I set my candle had a few mouldy books stacked in one corner, and its paint was covered with scratched writing. The writing consisted only of a name, repeated in every sort of lettering, large and small: _Catherine Earnshaw_, changed here and there to _Catherine Heathcliff_, and then to _Catherine Linton_.

With dull indifference I rested my head against the window and went on spelling out Catherine Earnshaw—Heathcliff—Linton until my eyes shut. They had been closed less than five minutes when blazing white letters sprang out of the dark, as vivid as ghosts: the air swarmed with Catherines. Rousing myself to drive away the intrusive name, I discovered that the wick of my candle had bent over onto one of the old books, filling the place with the scent of scorched calfskin.

I trimmed it off and, feeling thoroughly uncomfortable with cold and the remains of my nausea, sat up and opened the damaged volume across my knees. It was a Testament in thin print, with an awful musty smell. A blank leaf carried the inscription “Catherine Earnshaw, her book,” and a date about twenty-five years earlier.

I closed it and picked up another, then another, until I had inspected them all. Catherine's library was small and select, and the books' battered condition showed they had been well used, though not entirely for their proper purpose. Scarcely a chapter had escaped a pen-and-ink commentary—or what looked like one—filling every scrap of space the printer had left blank. Some passages were disconnected sentences; others made a regular diary, scrawled in an unformed child's handwriting. At the head of an extra page, probably a great treasure when first discovered, I was delighted to find an excellent caricature of my friend Joseph, roughly but forcefully drawn. I immediately felt interested in this unknown Catherine and began at once to make out her faded hieroglyphics.

“A dreadful Sunday,” began the paragraph below. “I wish my father would come back. Hindley is a hateful replacement—he treats Heathcliff horribly—H. and I mean to rebel—we made our first move this evening.

“Rain poured down all day, so we couldn't go to church. Joseph therefore had to organise a congregation in the attic, while Hindley and his wife lounged downstairs by a comfortable fire—doing anything but reading their Bibles, I'll swear. Heathcliff, the miserable ploughboy and I were ordered to take our prayer books and go up. There we sat in a row on a sack of grain, groaning and shivering, and hoping Joseph would shiver too, so he'd shorten the sermon for his own comfort. A useless hope! The service lasted exactly three hours, yet my brother had the nerve to exclaim as we came down, ‘What, finished already?’ We used to be allowed to play on Sunday evenings if we kept reasonably quiet; now the slightest giggle gets us sent into corners.

“‘You forget there's a master here,’ says the tyrant. ‘I'll destroy the first of you who makes me lose my temper! I demand absolute seriousness and silence. Ah, boy! Was that you? Frances, darling, pull his hair as you pass: I heard him snap his fingers.’ Frances pulled his hair with enthusiasm, then sat on her husband's knee, and there they stayed like a pair of babies, kissing and talking nonsense for hours—silly chatter we would have been ashamed of. We made ourselves as comfortable as we could in the arch under the dresser. I had just fastened our pinafores together and hung them up as a curtain when Joseph came in on an errand from the stables. He tears down my work, boxes my ears and croaks:

“‘T' master's nobbut just buried, and t' Sabbath isn't over, and t' sound o' t' gospel's still in yer ears, and ye dare go playing! Shame on ye! Sit ye down, wicked children! There's good books enough, if ye'll read 'em: sit down and think about yer souls!’

“With these words he forced us to arrange ourselves where a dull ray from the distant fire would let us read the rubbish he thrust on us. I could not stand the task. I grabbed my grimy volume by the spine and hurled it into the dog kennel, declaring I hated a good book. Heathcliff kicked his into the same place. Then there was an uproar!

“‘Master Hindley!’ our chaplain shouted. ‘Master, come here! Miss Cathy's torn t' back off “The Helmet o' Salvation,” and Heathcliff's kicked his foot into t' first part o' “The Broad Way to Destruction!” It's fair frightening ye let 'em carry on this way. Eh! T' old man would ha' thrashed 'em properly—but he's gone!’

“Hindley hurried from his paradise beside the fire, grabbed one of us by the collar and the other by the arm, and threw us both into the back kitchen. There, Joseph assured us, ‘old Nick’ would come for us as surely as we were alive. Comforted in this fashion, we each found a separate corner to await his arrival. I got this book and a pot of ink from a shelf and pushed the house door ajar for light. Writing has passed twenty minutes for me, but my companion is impatient. He suggests we take the dairymaid's cloak and run out over the moors under its shelter. A pleasant idea—and if the surly old man comes in, he can think his prophecy has come true. We can't get any wetter or colder in the rain than we are here.”
I suppose Catherine carried out her plan, because the next sentence turned to a different subject: she became tearful.

“I never imagined Hindley could make me cry so much!” she wrote. “My head aches until I can't bear it on the pillow, and still I can't stop. Poor Heathcliff! Hindley calls him a vagabond and won't let him sit or eat with us any more. He says we mustn't play together, and threatens to throw him out of the house if we disobey. He's been blaming our father—how dare he?—for treating H. too generously, and swears he'll put him back where he belongs—”

I began to nod over the faint writing, my eyes straying from the handwriting to the print. I saw a red, decorated title: “Seventy Times Seven, and the First of the Seventy-First. A Pious Discourse delivered by the Reverend Jabez Branderham, in the Chapel of Gimmerden Sough.” While I was still half-consciously puzzling over what Jabez Branderham would make of his subject, I sank back into bed and fell asleep. Alas, what bad tea and bad temper can do! What else could have given me such a dreadful night? I cannot remember another to compare with it in all the time I have been capable of suffering.

I started dreaming almost before I stopped knowing where I was. I thought it was morning and I had set out for home with Joseph as my guide. Snow lay yards deep along our road; as we struggled through it, my companion exhausted me with constant complaints that I had brought no pilgrim's staff. He said I could never get into the house without one, and proudly waved a heavy-headed club, which I understood was what he meant by that name. For a moment I thought it absurd to need such a weapon to enter my own home. Then a fresh idea struck me. We were not going there: we were on our way to hear the famous Jabez Branderham preach on the text “Seventy Times Seven.” Either Joseph, the preacher or I had committed the “First of the Seventy-First,” and was to be publicly exposed and cast out of the church.

We reached the chapel. I have actually passed it two or three times on my walks. It stands in a hollow between two hills—a high hollow near a marsh, whose peaty damp is said to preserve the few bodies buried there as well as embalming would. The roof has remained intact so far; but the minister's pay is only twenty pounds a year and a two-roomed house threatening shortly to collapse into one room, so no clergyman will take on the parish. This is particularly understandable given the common report that his flock would prefer to let him starve rather than add a penny from their own pockets to his income. In my dream, however, Jabez had a full and attentive congregation; and he preached—good God, what a sermon! It was divided into _four hundred and ninety_ parts, each as long as an ordinary sermon, and each dealing with a separate sin! Where he found them all I cannot say. He interpreted the phrase in his own way, and apparently the brother had to commit a different sin on every occasion. They were the strangest offences: peculiar transgressions I had never even imagined.

Oh, how tired I became. How I squirmed and yawned, nodded and woke again! How I pinched and pricked myself, rubbed my eyes, stood up, sat down, and nudged Joseph to ask whether the man would _ever_ finish. I was sentenced to hear it all. At last he reached the “_First of the Seventy-First_.” At this crisis a sudden inspiration came upon me: I felt called to rise and denounce Jabez Branderham as the sinner whose sin no Christian was obliged to forgive.

“Sir,” I cried, “sitting in these four walls without a break, I have endured and forgiven the four hundred and ninety divisions of your sermon. Seventy times seven times I have picked up my hat and prepared to leave—seventy times seven times you have absurdly forced me back into my seat. The four hundred and ninety-first is beyond endurance. Fellow sufferers, attack him! Pull him down and crush him to atoms, so that the place which knows him may know him no more!”

“_Thou art the Man!_” cried Jabez after a solemn pause, leaning over his cushion. “Seventy times seven times you twisted your face in yawns—seventy times seven I consulted my soul: behold, this is human weakness; this too may be forgiven! The First of the Seventy-First has arrived. Brothers, carry out the judgment written against him. Such honour have all His saints!”

At that last word the entire gathering raised their pilgrim's staffs and rushed together upon me. With no weapon to lift in my defence, I began wrestling for Joseph's, since he was my nearest and fiercest attacker. As the crowd surged together, several clubs crossed and blows meant for me struck other heads. Soon the whole chapel rang with blows and answering blows: every man's hand was against his neighbour. Branderham, unwilling to stand idle, poured out his zeal by hammering loudly on the wooden pulpit. Its boards answered so sharply that at last, to my inexpressible relief, they woke me. And what had suggested this tremendous uproar? What had played Jabez's part in the commotion? Only a fir branch touching my window as the wind howled past, rattling its dry cones against the panes! I listened uncertainly for a moment, identified the troublemaker, then turned over, dozed and dreamed again—if possible, more unpleasantly than before.

This time I remembered I was lying in the oak enclosure, and clearly heard the gusting wind and the driving snow. I also heard the fir branch repeating its irritating noise, and correctly recognised its cause; but it bothered me so much that I decided to silence it if I could. I thought I got up and tried to undo the window catch. The hook was soldered into its fastening, something I had noticed while awake but forgotten. “I must stop it all the same!” I muttered, driving my knuckles through the glass and reaching out to catch the troublesome branch. Instead my fingers closed around the fingers of a small, ice-cold hand!
The overwhelming horror of a nightmare seized me. I tried to pull my arm back, but the hand held on, and a voice full of misery sobbed,
“Let me in—let me in!”
“Who are you?” I demanded, struggling all the while to free myself.
“Catherine Linton,” came the shivering answer—why did I think of _Linton_? I had read _Earnshaw_ twenty times for every Linton—“I've come home: I lost my way on the moor!”

As it spoke, I dimly made out a child's face peering through the window. Fear made me cruel. Finding I could not shake the creature off, I dragged its wrist onto the broken glass and rubbed it backwards and forwards until blood ran down and soaked the bedclothes. Still it wailed, “Let me in!” and kept its stubborn grip, almost driving me mad with terror.
“How can I!” I said at last. “Let _me_ go, then, if you want me to let you inside!”
The fingers loosened. I jerked my hand back through the hole, quickly piled the books in a pyramid against it, and blocked my ears against the pitiful pleading.
I seemed to hold them shut for more than fifteen minutes; but the moment I listened again, that sorrowful cry was still moaning on!
“Go away!” I shouted. “I won't ever let you in, even if you beg for twenty years.”
“It has been twenty years,” the voice mourned. “Twenty years. I've wandered homeless for twenty years!”
Then a faint scratching began outside, and the pile of books shifted as though something were pushing it forward.
I tried to leap up but could not move a limb, and screamed aloud in a frenzy of terror.

To my embarrassment, I discovered that the scream was no dream. Quick footsteps came towards my bedroom; someone pushed the door open forcefully, and light shone through the square openings at the top of the bed. I was still sitting there shivering and wiping sweat from my forehead. The intruder seemed to hesitate, muttering to himself.
Finally he spoke in something near a whisper, clearly expecting no reply:
“Is somebody in here?”
I thought it best to admit I was there, recognising Heathcliff's voice and fearing he would search further if I stayed silent.
Accordingly I turned and slid the panels open. I will not readily forget the effect of that movement.

Heathcliff stood near the doorway in his shirt and trousers, candle wax dripping over his fingers, his face as white as the wall behind him. The first creak of the oak struck him like an electric shock. The candle flew several feet out of his hand, and he was so violently shaken that he could scarcely pick it up.

“It's only your guest, sir,” I called, wishing to spare him the humiliation of displaying more of his fear. “Unfortunately a dreadful nightmare made me scream in my sleep. I'm sorry to have disturbed you.”

“Oh, God damn you, Mr. Lockwood! I wish you were at the—” my host began, putting the candle on a chair because he could not hold it still. “And who brought you up to this room?” he went on, digging his nails into his palms and grinding his teeth to control his trembling jaws. “Who was it? I've a good mind to throw them out of the house this instant!”

“Your servant Zillah,” I answered, jumping onto the floor and hurriedly getting dressed. “I wouldn't object if you did, Mr. Heathcliff; she thoroughly deserves it. I suppose she wanted further proof that the room was haunted, at my expense. Well, it is—it's crawling with ghosts and goblins! You're quite right to keep it locked up, I assure you. Nobody will thank you for a nap in a den like this!”

“What are you talking about?” Heathcliff asked. “And what are you doing? Lie down and spend the rest of the night here, since you _are_ here; but for Heaven's sake! Don't make that horrible noise again: nothing could justify it unless someone was cutting your throat!”

“If that little devil had come through the window, she'd probably have strangled me!” I retorted. “I won't put up with your hospitable ancestors tormenting me again. Wasn't the Reverend Jabez Branderham a relation on your mother's side? And that minx, Catherine Linton or Earnshaw, or whatever her name was—she must have been a changeling—wicked little soul! She told me she'd wandered the earth for twenty years: a deserved punishment for her sins in life, I've no doubt!”

Almost as soon as I had spoken, I remembered how Heathcliff's name was joined to Catherine's in the book. That fact had entirely escaped my memory until my words recalled it. I blushed at my thoughtlessness, but hurried to add, without otherwise acknowledging my offence, “The truth is, sir, I spent the first part of the night—” Here I stopped again. I had been about to say “reading those old books,” which would have revealed my knowledge of their handwritten contents as well as the print. I corrected myself and continued: “spelling out the name scratched on that window ledge. A monotonous pastime, likely to send me to sleep, like counting, or—”

“What _can_ you mean, speaking like this to _me!_” Heathcliff thundered with savage force. “How—how _dare_ you, beneath my own roof?—God! He must be mad to speak so!” And he struck his forehead in fury.

I could not decide whether to take offence or continue explaining; but he seemed so deeply affected that I pitied him and went on describing my dreams. I insisted I had never heard the name “Catherine Linton” before; reading it repeatedly had merely left an impression which took human form when I no longer controlled my imagination. While I spoke, Heathcliff gradually retreated behind the bed, finally sitting down almost hidden by it. From his uneven, broken breathing, however, I guessed he was struggling to master a surge of violent feeling. Unwilling to show that I had heard this struggle, I noisily continued dressing, consulted my watch and talked to myself about the length of the night. “Not three yet! I could have sworn it was six. Time stands still here: surely we must have gone to bed at eight!”

“Always nine in winter, and up at four,” my host answered, stifling a groan and, if I read the shadow of his moving arm correctly, brushing a tear from his eyes. “Mr. Lockwood,” he added, “you can use my room. You'll only be in the way if you go downstairs so early, and that childish screaming has sent all chance of sleep to the devil for me.”

“And for me,” I replied. “I'll walk round the yard until daylight, then leave. You needn't fear another intrusion. I'm thoroughly cured now of looking for pleasure in company, whether in the country or the town. A sensible man ought to find enough companionship in himself.”

“Charming company!” Heathcliff muttered. “Take the candle and go wherever you want. I'll join you shortly. Keep out of the yard, though: the dogs are loose; and in the sitting room—Juno stands guard there, and—no, you can only wander along the passages and stairs. But go on! I'll come in two minutes!”

I obeyed far enough to leave the room, but, not knowing where the narrow passages led, I stood still. Thus I unwillingly witnessed an act of superstition from my landlord oddly at variance with his apparent good sense. He climbed onto the bed and wrenched open the window, breaking into an uncontrollable storm of tears as he pulled at it. “Come in! Come in!” he sobbed. “Cathy, please come. Oh, do—_once_ more! Oh! My heart's darling! Hear me _this_ time, Catherine, at last!” The ghost displayed the usual wilfulness of ghosts: it gave no sign of existing. But wind and snow whirled wildly inside, reaching even where I stood and blowing out the candle.

The flood of grief accompanying his ravings held such anguish that pity made me forget their foolishness. I withdrew, half angry at having heard anything, and upset that I had told him my ridiculous nightmare and caused such agony—although _why_ it had done so was beyond me. I cautiously made my way downstairs and arrived in the back kitchen, where a little glow from the fire, raked together into a compact heap, allowed me to relight my candle. Nothing moved except a grey tabby cat, which crept out of the ashes and greeted me with a complaining mew.

Two curved benches almost enclosed the hearth. I stretched out on one, and Grimalkin climbed onto the other. We were both nodding before anyone disturbed our retreat. It was Joseph, shuffling down a wooden ladder that disappeared through a hatch in the roof—the way to his attic, I suppose. He gave a dark look at the small flame I had coaxed up between the bars, swept the cat from its perch, and sat in its place to begin packing tobacco into a three-inch pipe. My presence in his sanctuary was evidently an impertinence too disgraceful for words: he silently put the pipe between his lips, folded his arms and puffed away. I let him enjoy this luxury undisturbed; and after drawing out the final curl of smoke and giving a deep sigh, he rose and left as solemnly as he had arrived.

Next came a livelier footstep. I opened my mouth to say good morning but shut it again before delivering the greeting, for Hareton Earnshaw was saying his prayers _sotto voce_ in a succession of curses against everything he touched. He was rummaging in a corner for a spade or shovel to dig through the snowdrifts. He glanced over the back of the bench, nostrils flaring, and no more considered exchanging courtesies with me than with my companion the cat. His preparations suggested to me that going outside was permitted; I left my hard bed and moved to follow. Seeing this, he pushed at an inner door with the end of his spade and made an inarticulate noise to indicate that this was where I must go if I wanted a change of place.

The door opened into the sitting room, where the women were already at work: Zillah driving tongues of flame up the chimney with an enormous pair of bellows, and Mrs. Heathcliff kneeling on the hearth, reading by the blaze. She held a hand between her eyes and the furnace heat and seemed entirely absorbed in her book. She paused only to scold the servant for showering her with sparks, or occasionally to push away a dog thrusting its nosing muzzle too boldly into her face. I was surprised to find Heathcliff there too. He stood facing the fire, his back to me, just finishing a furious scene with poor Zillah. Every now and then she stopped working to lift a corner of her apron and let out an indignant groan.

“And you, you worthless—” he burst out as I entered, turning to his daughter-in-law and using an animal name as harmless as duck or sheep, though usually printed as a dash—. “There you are, up to your idle tricks again! The others earn their food—you live on my charity! Put that rubbish away and find yourself some work. You'll pay me for the torment of having you always before my eyes—do you hear, you damned hussy?”

“I'll put my rubbish away because you can force me if I don't,” the young woman answered, shutting her book and throwing it onto a chair. “But even if you swear your tongue out, I won't do anything except what I choose!”

Heathcliff raised a hand, and she sprang out of reach, evidently familiar with its weight. Having no desire to watch a cat-and-dog fight, I stepped briskly forward as though eager for the warmth of the fire and entirely unaware of the quarrel I had interrupted. Both had enough manners to stop fighting. Heathcliff put his fists in his pockets, away from temptation; Mrs. Heathcliff curled her lip and went to a distant chair, where she kept her promise by acting the statue for the rest of my visit. That was brief. I refused breakfast and at the first hint of dawn seized a chance to escape into the open air, now clear, still and as cold as invisible ice.

Before I reached the far end of the garden my landlord called for me to stop and offered to guide me over the moor. It was fortunate he did: the whole hillside was a rolling white ocean, its rises and hollows giving no reliable sign of the ground beneath. Many pits, at least, had been filled level, and entire ridges of quarry waste had vanished from the map left in my mind by yesterday's walk. I had noticed a line of upright stones beside the road, six or seven yards apart, running the whole length of the waste. These had been set up and coated with lime expressly to guide travellers in darkness, and when snow like this blurred the distinction between the firm path and the deep bogs on either side. Now, apart from a dirty point sticking up here and there, every trace of them had disappeared. My companion often had to tell me to bear right or left when I thought I was faithfully following the road's curves.

We spoke very little. At the entrance to Thrushcross Park he stopped, saying I could not go wrong from there. A hurried bow served for our farewells, and I pressed on using my own judgment, for the gatekeeper's lodge is still empty. It is two miles from the gate to the Grange; I believe I made it four by losing my way among the trees and sinking into snow up to my neck—a situation only those who have experienced it can appreciate. Whatever route I took, the clock was striking twelve when I entered the house: exactly one hour for every mile of the usual journey from Wuthering Heights.

My human fixture and her satellites rushed to greet me, exclaiming all at once that they had entirely given me up. Everyone had assumed I had died during the night, and they were wondering how to begin searching for my remains. I told them to be quiet now they could see I had returned, and dragged myself upstairs, numb to the heart. After changing into dry clothes and pacing up and down for thirty or forty minutes to restore my body's warmth, I retired to my study as weak as a kitten—almost too weak to enjoy the cheerful fire and steaming coffee the servant had prepared to revive me.

chapters.title: Chapter IV
paragraphs: What foolish weathercocks we are! I had resolved to keep myself free of all human company and thanked my lucky stars for finding a place where company was almost impossible. Yet I, weak creature, after struggling with loneliness and low spirits until dusk, finally had to surrender. Pretending I needed information about running the household, I asked Mrs. Dean to sit with me when she brought my supper. I sincerely hoped she would turn out to be an inveterate gossip, whose talk would either restore my spirits or send me to sleep.
“You've lived here a long time,” I began. “Didn't you say sixteen years?”
“Eighteen, sir. I came to look after the mistress when she married; after her death, the master kept me on as his housekeeper.”
“Really.”

A silence followed. I feared she was no gossip, unless it concerned her own affairs, which could hardly interest me. But after sitting in thought for a while, a fist on each knee and a thoughtful cloud over her rosy face, she exclaimed, “Ah, things have changed a great deal since then!”
“Yes,” I observed, “I suppose you've witnessed quite a few changes?”
“I have, and troubles along with them,” she replied.

“Ah, I'll bring up my landlord's family!” I thought. “A promising subject to begin with! And I'd like to hear about that pretty young widow: whether she was born here, or, more probably, is a foreign growth that the surly _indigenae_—the natives—refuse to recognise as one of their own.” With that purpose, I asked Mrs. Dean why Heathcliff rented out Thrushcross Grange and chose to live in a house and location so much beneath it. “Does he lack the money to keep this estate in good order?” I asked.

“Money, sir!” she answered. “Nobody knows how much he has, and there's more every year. Yes, yes, he can afford a grander house than this, but he's very tight—close-fisted. Even if he'd intended to move to Thrushcross Grange, once he heard of a good tenant he couldn't have passed up the chance of a few hundred pounds more. It's strange how greedy people can be when they've nobody else in the world!”
“Apparently he had a son?”
“Yes, he had one son—now he's dead.”
“And the young woman, Mrs. Heathcliff, is that son's widow?”
“Yes.”
“Where was she from in the first place?”

“Why, sir, she's my late master's daughter. Before her marriage she was Catherine Linton. I was her nurse, poor thing! I did hope Mr. Heathcliff would move here; then she and I might have been together again.”

“What! Catherine Linton?” I exclaimed in astonishment. A moment's thought, though, persuaded me that this was not my ghostly Catherine. “Then,” I went on, “the previous occupant here was called Linton?”
“Yes, he was.”
“And who is Earnshaw—Hareton Earnshaw, the young man living with Mr. Heathcliff? Are the two related?”
“No. He's the late Mrs. Linton's nephew.”
“So he's the young woman's cousin?”
“Yes, and her husband was her cousin too: one on her mother's side, the other on her father's. Heathcliff married Mr. Linton's sister.”
“I noticed ‘Earnshaw’ carved above the front door at Wuthering Heights. Is the family an old one?”
“Very old, sir; and Hareton is the last of them, just as our Miss Cathy is the last of us—I mean the Lintons. Have you visited Wuthering Heights? Forgive my asking, but I'd like to know how she is!”
“Mrs. Heathcliff? She looked quite healthy and very lovely, though I think she wasn't especially happy.”
“Oh dear, that doesn't surprise me! And what did you think of the master?”
“A rather rough sort, Mrs. Dean. Isn't that what people say of him?”
“Rough as a saw and hard as whinstone rock! The less you have to do with him, the better.”
“Life must have given him some ups and downs to make him so disagreeable. Do you know his story?”

“It's the story of a cuckoo, sir. I know all of it, except where he was born, who his parents were, and how he first got his money. And Hareton's been pushed out like a dunnock fledgling before it can fly! That unlucky lad is the only person in this parish who doesn't suspect how he's been cheated.”
“Well, Mrs. Dean, telling me about my neighbours would be an act of kindness. I don't think I could sleep if I went to bed, so please sit and talk for an hour.”
“Of course, sir! I'll get some sewing, then sit for as long as you like. But you've caught a cold: I saw you shaking, and you must have some gruel to drive it away.”

The good woman bustled out, and I huddled closer to the fire. My head was hot and the rest of me cold; besides, my nerves and brain were excited almost to the point of absurdity. This did not make me uncomfortable so much as afraid—as I still am—that today's and yesterday's adventures might have serious consequences. Soon she returned with a steaming bowl and a sewing basket. She put the bowl on the hearth and drew her chair closer, evidently pleased to find me so ready for company.

Before I came here, she began, without waiting for another invitation to tell her story, I was nearly always at Wuthering Heights. My mother had nursed Mr. Hindley Earnshaw—Hareton's father—and I grew used to playing with the children. I ran errands too, helped with the haymaking, and stayed about the farm ready to do whatever anyone found for me. One fine summer morning, at the start of harvest, I remember, old Mr. Earnshaw came downstairs dressed for a journey. After telling Joseph what work needed doing that day, he turned to Hindley, Cathy and me, for I was eating porridge with them, and said to his son, “Now, my bonny lad, I'm going to Liverpool today. What shall I bring you? Choose what you like, only keep it small, because I'm walking there and back: sixty miles each way, and that's a long stretch!” Hindley asked for a fiddle. Then he asked Miss Cathy, who was barely six but could ride any horse in the stable; she chose a whip. He remembered me too: his heart was kind, though sometimes he was rather strict. He promised me a pocketful of apples and pears, then kissed his children, said goodbye and set off.

Those three days he was away seemed a long time to all of us, and little Cathy often asked when he would come home. Mrs. Earnshaw expected him by supper on the third evening and delayed the meal hour after hour. Still there was no sign of him, and at last the children tired of running to the gate to look. Darkness fell. She wanted them in bed, but they pleaded so sadly to stay up that she let them. At about eleven the latch lifted quietly and the master stepped inside. He dropped into a chair, laughing and groaning, and told everyone to stand back: he was nearly dead, and wouldn't make another walk like that for the three kingdoms.

“And to be scolded to death at the end of it!” he said, unfolding the greatcoat bundled in his arms. “Look here, wife! Nothing in my life has worn me out like this. But you must take it as a gift from God, though it's almost as dark as if it came from the devil.”

We crowded around. Over Miss Cathy's head I glimpsed a dirty, ragged child with black hair, big enough to walk and talk—its face actually looked older than Catherine's. Yet when it was put on its feet it only stared round and kept repeating some gibberish nobody could understand. I was frightened; Mrs. Earnshaw was ready to throw it outside. She flew into a rage, asking how he could bring that gypsy brat into the house when they had their own children to feed and provide for. What did he intend to do with it? Was he mad? The master tried to explain, but he really was half dead with exhaustion. Through her scolding I could make out only that he had seen it starving and homeless, and practically unable to speak, in the streets of Liverpool. He had picked it up and asked who it belonged to. Nobody knew, he said; and as he had little time or money to spare, he thought it better to bring it straight home than incur useless expenses there, since he was determined not to abandon it as he had found it. Well, in the end my mistress grumbled herself quiet, and Mr. Earnshaw told me to wash it, find clean clothes for it and let it sleep with the children.

Hindley and Cathy were content to watch and listen until peace returned. Then they both searched their father's pockets for the promised presents. Hindley was fourteen, but when he pulled out what remained of a fiddle, crushed to pieces inside the greatcoat, he burst into noisy tears. Cathy, discovering that the master had lost her whip while caring for the stranger, showed her temper by baring her teeth and spitting at the uncomprehending little thing. For this she earned a hard blow from her father, to teach her better manners. They absolutely refused to let it share their bed, or even their room. I had no more sense than they did, so I left it on the stair landing, hoping it might be gone by morning. By chance, or perhaps drawn by the sound of his voice, it crept to Mr. Earnshaw's door, where he found it when he came out. He asked how it got there. I had to confess, and was sent away from the house as punishment for my cowardice and cruelty.

That was how Heathcliff first entered the family. When I came back a few days later—for I did not consider my banishment permanent—I found they had named him “Heathcliff,” after a son who had died in childhood. Ever since, it has served him as both first name and surname. He and Miss Cathy were now close friends, but Hindley hated him, and, truthfully, so did I. We tormented and persecuted him shamefully: I lacked the sense to recognise my unfairness, and our mistress never said a word for him when she saw him mistreated.

He seemed a sullen, enduring child, perhaps already hardened to abuse. He took Hindley's blows without a flinch or a tear, and when I pinched him he only drew a breath and opened his eyes, as though he had hurt himself accidentally and nobody was responsible. Such endurance enraged old Earnshaw whenever he caught his son tormenting what he called the poor fatherless child. He grew strangely fond of Heathcliff and believed everything he said—though to be fair, the boy said very little, and usually told the truth. He indulged him much more than Cathy, who was too mischievous and wilful to be a favourite.

So he created ill feeling in the house from the start. By the time Mrs. Earnshaw died, less than two years later, the young master had come to see his father as a tyrant rather than a friend, and Heathcliff as someone who had stolen his father's affection and his own privileges. Brooding over these wrongs made him bitter. For a while I sympathised, but I changed my mind when the children caught measles and I had to nurse them, taking on a grown woman's responsibilities all at once. Heathcliff was dangerously ill and, at his worst, wanted me constantly beside his pillow. I suppose he realised how much I did for him and did not have the sense to see I was obliged to do it. But I will say this: no nurse ever looked after a quieter child. The contrast with the others forced me to be fairer. Cathy and her brother pestered me dreadfully; _he_ was as uncomplaining as a lamb, though it was hardness rather than gentleness that made him so little trouble.

He recovered, and the doctor said it was largely thanks to me, praising my care. His praise made me vain and softened me towards the creature through whom I had earned it, so Hindley lost his last supporter. Still, I could not be devoted to Heathcliff, and often wondered what my master found so admirable in that sullen boy, who, as far as I remember, never repaid his kindness with any sign of gratitude. He was not rude to his benefactor, simply unfeeling, although he knew perfectly well how strongly he held his affection and that he need only speak for the whole household to bow to his wishes. For example, I remember Mr. Earnshaw buying two young horses at the parish fair and giving one to each boy. Heathcliff chose the better-looking one, but it soon went lame. When he discovered this, he told Hindley—

“You'll have to swap horses with me. I don't like mine; and if you won't, I'll tell your father about the three beatings you've given me this week and show him my arm: it's black all the way to the shoulder.” Hindley stuck his tongue out and struck him about the ears. “You'd better do it now,” he insisted, retreating to the doorway—they were in the stable. “You'll have to; and if I mention these blows, you'll get them back with interest.” “Get out, dog!” Hindley shouted, threatening him with an iron weight used for weighing hay and potatoes. “Throw it,” he answered, standing his ground, “and I'll tell him how you boasted you'd throw me out as soon as he died. See if he doesn't throw you out at once.” Hindley hurled it, striking him in the chest. He fell, but immediately struggled upright, pale and breathless. If I had not stopped him, he would have gone straight to the master and taken full revenge by letting his condition speak for him and indicating who had caused it. “Take my colt then, Gypsy!” young Earnshaw said. “And I pray he breaks your neck. Take him and be damned, you beggarly intruder! Coax my father out of everything he's got; only show him afterwards what you are, you little devil.—And take that! I hope the horse kicks your brains out!”

Heathcliff had gone to untie the horse and move it into his own stall. As he passed behind it, Hindley ended his speech by knocking him beneath its feet, then ran away as fast as he could without waiting to see whether his wishes came true. I was surprised how calmly the child picked himself up and went on with his plan, exchanging the saddles and everything else. Afterwards he sat on a bundle of hay until the sickness caused by the heavy blow passed, before going into the house. I easily persuaded him to let me blame the horse for his bruises: he cared little what story was told, now he had what he wanted. Indeed, he complained so rarely about disturbances like these that I really believed he was not revengeful. As you will hear, I was completely mistaken.

chapters.title: Chapter V
paragraphs: As time passed, Mr. Earnshaw's health began to fail. He had been active and healthy, but his strength deserted him suddenly; and once confined to his corner by the fire, he became painfully irritable. The smallest thing upset him, and any suspected challenge to his authority almost sent him into fits. This was particularly noticeable when anyone tried to cheat or bully his favourite. He guarded the boy anxiously against even an unkind word, apparently convinced that because he himself loved Heathcliff, everyone else hated him and wanted to do him harm. This did the boy no good. The kinder people among us did not want to distress the master, so we indulged his favouritism, and that indulgence fed the child's pride and dark moods richly. Yet it became almost unavoidable. Two or three times Hindley showed his contempt in his father's presence and drove the old man into a rage: he snatched up his stick to strike him, then trembled with fury because he lacked the strength.

At last our curate advised sending the young man to college. We had a curate then who made the income sufficient by teaching the little Lintons and Earnshaws and working his own small piece of land. Mr. Earnshaw agreed, though sorrowfully, saying, “Hindley's good for nothing, and he'll never prosper wherever he wanders.”

I sincerely hoped we would have peace now. It distressed me to think the master's good deed had made him miserable. I imagined the discontent of his age and illness came from his quarrels with the family, as he insisted it did; but really, sir, it came from his failing body. Even so, we might have managed reasonably well except for two people: Miss Cathy and Joseph, the servant whom I expect you saw up there. He was, and most likely still is, the most tiresome, self-righteous Pharisee ever to rummage through a Bible, gathering its promises for himself and throwing its curses at his neighbours. His talent for sermons and pious conversation made a deep impression on Mr. Earnshaw, and the weaker the master grew, the more power Joseph gained. He never stopped pestering him about his soul and the need to govern his children strictly. He encouraged him to see Hindley as a hopeless sinner, and every night grumbled through a long list of complaints against Catherine and Heathcliff, always taking care to flatter Earnshaw's weakness by putting the greater blame on her.

Certainly she had habits I had never seen in any other child. Fifty times a day, and more, she tried every one of us beyond patience: from the moment she came downstairs until she went to bed, we could never count on a minute without mischief. Her spirits were always at high tide and her tongue never stopped—singing, laughing and teasing everyone who would not join her. She was a wild, wicked little thing, but had the loveliest eyes, sweetest smile and lightest step in the parish. After all, I believe she meant no harm: once she made you truly cry, she nearly always cried along with you and forced you to stop so that you could comfort her. She was far too fond of Heathcliff. The worst punishment we could devise was keeping her away from him, yet she was scolded on his account more than any of us. When playing, she loved being the little mistress, giving orders and using her hands freely on her companions. She tried it on me, but I would not put up with being slapped and commanded, and I let her know it.

Now Mr. Earnshaw could not take a joke from his children: he had always been serious and strict with them. Catherine, for her part, could not understand why illness should make her father crosser and less patient than when he was strong. His peevish rebukes gave her a naughty pleasure in provoking him. Nothing delighted her more than all of us scolding her together while she defied us with a bold, impudent look and a quick reply, mocking Joseph's religious curses and tormenting me. She also did the thing her father hated most: she showed that her pretend bullying, which he took seriously, had more power over Heathcliff than his kindness did. The boy would do anything _she_ ordered, and what _he_ ordered only when he felt inclined. Sometimes, after behaving as badly as possible all day, she came affectionately to make peace at night. “No, Cathy,” the old man would say, “I can't love thee; thou'rt worse than thy brother. Go and say thy prayers, child, and ask God's forgiveness. I fear thy mother and I must regret ever bringing thee up!” At first this made her cry; but constant rejection hardened her, and she laughed when I told her to apologise for her faults and ask to be forgiven.

At last the hour arrived that ended Mr. Earnshaw's earthly troubles. One October evening he died quietly in his chair beside the fire. A strong wind battered the house and roared down the chimney. It sounded wild and stormy, but the air was not cold and we were all together. I sat a little way from the hearth with my knitting, and Joseph read his Bible near the table: in those days the servants usually sat in the main room once their work was finished. Miss Cathy had been ill, which kept her quiet. She leaned against her father's knee, with Heathcliff lying on the floor, his head in her lap. I remember the master stroking her lovely hair before he dozed off—seeing her gentle was a rare pleasure for him—and asking, “Why can't thou always be a good lass, Cathy?” She looked up into his face, laughed and answered, “Why can't you always be a good man, father?” But when she saw him grow annoyed again, she kissed his hand and promised to sing him to sleep. She began very softly, until his fingers slipped from hers and his head dropped onto his chest. I told her to be quiet and keep still in case she woke him. We all remained as silent as mice for a full half-hour, and would have stayed so longer, but Joseph finished his chapter, rose, and said he must wake the master for prayers and bed. He went over, spoke his name and touched his shoulder, but he did not stir. Joseph took the candle and looked at him. I sensed something was wrong when he put the light down and, taking each child by an arm, whispered that they should “get upstairs and make little noise—they could pray on their own tonight—he'd summat to do.”

“I'll say goodnight to father first,” Catherine said, throwing her arms round his neck before we could stop her. The poor thing understood her loss at once and screamed, “Oh, he's dead, Heathcliff! He's dead!” Then both children began crying with heartbreaking grief.

I wept loudly and bitterly with them, but Joseph demanded what we meant by making such a noise over a saint in heaven. He told me to put on my cloak and run to Gimmerton for the doctor and the parson. I could not see what use either could be by then. Still, I went through the wind and rain and brought one of them, the doctor, back with me; the other promised to come in the morning. Leaving Joseph to explain, I ran up to the children's room. Their door stood ajar, and I saw they had not gone to bed, although it was after midnight. They were calmer now and did not need my comfort. The little souls were consoling each other with better thoughts than I could have found. No parson ever described heaven as beautifully as their innocent talk did; and while I listened and sobbed, I could not help wishing we were all safely there together.

chapters.title: Chapter VI
paragraphs: Mr. Hindley returned for the funeral, bringing a wife—a surprise that astonished us and set the whole neighbourhood gossiping. He never told us who she was or where she came from. She probably had neither money nor family standing to recommend her, or he would hardly have hidden the marriage from his father.

Left to herself, she would not have caused much disturbance in the household. From the moment she crossed the threshold, everything she saw and everything happening around her seemed to delight her, except the preparations for the burial and the mourners' presence. Her behaviour then made me think she was half foolish. She rushed to her room and made me accompany her, though I ought to have been dressing the children. There she sat shaking and wringing her hands, asking over and over, “Have they gone yet?” Then she began describing hysterically how the sight of black clothes affected her, starting and trembling until she burst into tears. When I asked what was wrong, she said she did not know: she was simply so afraid of dying! I thought her no more likely to die than myself. She was rather thin, but young and fresh-faced, with eyes sparkling like diamonds. Admittedly, I noticed that climbing the stairs made her breathe rapidly, that any sudden noise sent her trembling, and that she sometimes had a troublesome cough. But I knew nothing of what such signs foretold and felt no urge to sympathise. We generally don't take to outsiders here, Mr. Lockwood, unless they take to us first.

Young Earnshaw had changed a good deal during his three years away. He was thinner and paler and spoke and dressed quite differently. The very day he returned he told Joseph and me that from then on we must keep to the back kitchen and leave the sitting room to him. In fact, he would have had a small spare room papered and carpeted to make a parlour; but his wife was so pleased with the white floor and enormous glowing fireplace, the pewter dishes, the dresser of crockery, the dog kennel and the space for moving about in their usual room that he decided she did not need the change for her comfort and abandoned it.

She was delighted, too, to discover a sister among her new acquaintances. At first she chatted to Catherine, kissed her, ran about with her and showered her with presents. Her affection soon wore out, however, and when she became irritable, Hindley became tyrannical. A few words from her expressing a dislike of Heathcliff awakened all his old hatred of the boy. He expelled him from their company to live with the servants, stopped his lessons with the curate, and ordered him to work outside instead, making him labour as hard as any other boy on the farm.

At first Heathcliff endured his lowered position fairly well, because Cathy passed on her lessons to him and worked or played beside him in the fields. Both seemed likely to grow up as uncivilised as savages. The young master cared nothing about their behaviour or activities so long as they stayed out of his way. He would not even have bothered about their attendance at church on Sundays if Joseph and the curate had not reproached him for neglect whenever they were absent. That reminded him to order a beating for Heathcliff and the loss of dinner or supper for Catherine.
